analysis.one_liner: Bans new federal leases for offshore oil and gas drilling and for coal, oil, and gas on public land.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee on December 18, 2024 and died there 16 days later when the 118th Congress ended, with no hearing, no vote, and no action beyond its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the Interior Department from selling or renewing leases to extract oil, gas, and coal from federally controlled waters and land, including all offshore areas and existing leases in the Arctic seas, with narrow exceptions for national security and contract obligations. It was introduced by Rep. Jared Huffman and six Democratic cosponsors in the last weeks of the 118th Congress, referred to the Natural Resources Committee, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the main beneficiaries would be people exposed to climate change and to pollution from offshore drilling and coal mining—coastal communities, fishermen, and tribal nations near the Arctic seas whose existing leases would be canceled. Future generations would gain from keeping an estimated 90 percent of the potential emissions from federal fossil fuels underground. Taxpayers would also avoid subsidizing extraction on public land at below-market rates.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal communities, tribes, and anyone exposed to fossil fuel pollution

how_it_helps.text: It prohibits any new federal oil and gas leasing in the Arctic, Atlantic, Pacific, Gulf of Mexico, and all other outer Continental Shelf waters, including renewals of nonproducing leases.
It bars new federal coal, oil, tar sands, oil shale, and gas leases onshore, and bars renewing or extending nonproducing leases.
It cancels existing offshore leases in the Beaufort Sea, Cook Inlet, and Chukchi Sea within 60 days of enactment.
Its stated basis is that ending new federal fossil fuel leases would prevent about 90 percent of potential emissions from federal fossil fuels, helping avoid the most dangerous climate impacts.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on fossil fuel companies that depend on federal leases—oil and gas producers offshore and on public land, and coal operators—along with communities and workers whose jobs depend on that extraction, since the bill includes no transition assistance for them. Energy consumers could face somewhat higher prices if federal supply curtailment tightened markets.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil, gas, and coal companies on federal land

drawbacks.text: The bill would cancel existing offshore leases within 60 days of enactment, raising the prospect of large legal claims for breach of contract and taking of private leasehold interests.

By ending new federal leases and renewals of nonproducing leases, it would reduce future domestic oil, gas, and coal production, which critics say could raise energy prices and cost jobs in producing regions unless paired with transition support—which this bill does not provide.
Its national-security and contract-breach exceptions give the Interior Secretary significant discretion to carve out leases, a flexibility that could undercut the bill's stated aim.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill advanced a real public goal—cutting emissions from federal fossil fuels, which the bill's findings say account for a large share of the emissions compatible with 2°C warming [S2]—but it never got any committee or floor action in a Congress controlled by an opposing-party House, so its benefits were never weighed in a hearing or vote. Its most aggressive provision, canceling existing offshore leases within 60 days, would likely have drawn years of litigation and compensated takings claims from leaseholders, and its restrictions on renewing nonproducing leases would have raised costs for energy production on federal land. On the other side, the status quo that prevailed—continued leasing—carries the climate and local environmental costs the bill aimed to stop.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the House in mid-December 2024, referred to the Natural Resources Committee, and the Congress ended sixteen days later without any further action.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Huffman introduced the bill on December 18, 2024, the final month of the 118th Congress.
It was referred the same day to the House Natural Resources Committee, whose agenda it never reached.
No hearing, markup, or vote ever took place before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
It attracted six cosponsors, all Democrats, out of 216 House Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel companies with federal leases keep the existing system of federal leasing, renewals, and extensions, since no restriction was ever enacted.

for.name: Rep. Jared Huffman
for.role: Sponsor, House Natural Resources Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in December 2024, his final month of the 118th Congress.

for.name: 6 of 216 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Tlaib, Ocasio-Cortez, Carbajal, Jayapal, Garcia of Illinois, McGovern)

sides.party_line_note: All seven supporters were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-controlled House agenda never advanced it.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies operating on federal lands and waters
industries.note: The bill ends new federal leases and renewals of nonproducing leases offshore and onshore, and cancels existing Arctic-area offshore leases, cutting off future federal acreage. Producing leases in hand would not be directly shut down, but the pipeline of new federal supply ends.

industries.industry: Coal mining companies with federal leases
industries.note: No new federal coal leases, renewals, or lease reoffers for expiring leases, ending expansion on public land.

industries.industry: Coastal and fishing communities and tourism/recreation industries
industries.note: The bill's findings argue climate change already harms farming, fishing, forestry, and recreation, and that these communities would benefit from reduced offshore drilling risk and slower warming.
